# High-level goal

The circadian clock is the internal biological timer that keeps sleep, body temperature and other functions on a cycle of about 24 hours, and it is set each day mainly by light. I am conducting a population genomics project (POLYCLOCK) to investigate whether the human circadian clock has adapted to regional light and temperature regimes. For this class project, I will build a Shiny application, an interactive web page written in R where the reader changes the figures with controls such as sliders and menus. It will visualize the geographic and climatic structure of `r n_pops` human populations, to assess whether the data and study design can answer this question before proceeding with genetic analysis.

# Goals and motivation

Three things determine whether it is possible to answer POLYCLOCK’s research question, and none of them requires genetic data to check. First, climate must be distinguishable from ancestry (how closely populations are related), because both follow geography and either could explain a genetic difference between populations. Second, temperature has to be separable from day length (measured as the annual photoperiod range, the difference in hours between the longest and shortest day of the year), because both vary with latitude. Third, the coordinates of the populations have to be precise enough for climate maps with a resolution of about 1 km.

These are questions related to data structure and precision, and a table or a single statistic hides the answer. A table containing `r n_pops` populations and climate variables does not show whether climate groupings align with continental ones. A correlation between temperature and day length gives a single number, when what matters is which populations depart from the pattern. And a single climate value per population hides whether that value depends on coordinate precision: `r n_whole` of the `r n_pops` coordinates are recorded only to the nearest whole degree, so the true location may be tens of kilometers away, in a different climate. The final result is a small Shiny application with interactive figures that let readers explore these questions for themselves.

# Data

All datasets are real and publicly available, and I have already downloaded and processed them.

| Dataset | What it provides | Why this dataset |
|---------------------|--------------------------|--------------------------|
| [gnomAD v3.1.2 HGDP + 1000 Genomes (1KG) metadata](https://gnomad.broadinstitute.org/news/2021-10-gnomad-v3-1-2-minor-release) (Koenig et al. 2024), with Bergström et al. (2020) population annotations | Population names, regions, sample sizes and population coordinates | The Human Genome Diversity Project (HGDP) is one of the most geographically diverse samples of sequenced human populations, and every population has a recorded location |
| [WorldClim 2.1 bioclimatic variables](https://www.worldclim.org/data/bioclim.html) (Fick and Hijmans 2017) | Annual mean temperature, temperature seasonality, mean temperature of the warmest and coldest quarters, annual precipitation, at 30 arc-seconds (\~1 km) | Standard global climate surfaces, fine enough to test how much coordinate precision matters |

The metadata file and the climate maps are downloaded by scripts in the repository (`scripts/00_download_metadata.R` and `scripts/02_climate_data.R`); the file address and access date are in the References. Day length is not downloaded: the annual photoperiod range is calculated from each population's latitude with the model of Forsythe et al. (1995). Every column of the raw and derived files is described in the codebook (data dictionary) in `data/README.md`.

The HGDP part of the metadata covers `r format(n_people, big.mark = ",")` individuals in `r n_pops` populations from `r n_regions` regions. The populations sit at `r n_sites` distinct sites: Balochi and Brahui have the same recorded coordinates, as do Druze and Palestinian, so each pair is assigned one climate. The metadata also carries an older set of population columns with no published description. It treats Papuan Highlands and Papuan Sepik as one population, and Han and Northern Han as another, although the populations in each pair live in different climates. Its coordinates for three populations also do not match those of Bergström et al. (2020). I therefore use only the Bergström et al. (2020) columns. One population, Adygei, has recorded coordinates in the Black Sea, where the climate maps have no values. Its 10 km circle is also entirely sea. To keep all `r n_pops` populations in every figure, I will use its 25 km circle mean (land cells only) as its point value, and flag it in the figures.

# Research questions

While POLYCLOCK asks whether the human circadian clock has adapted to climate, answering that requires genetic data that this project does not include. My focus is the preliminary question of whether the POLYCLOCK study design can answer it. That depends on three things.

1.  **How far is climate confounded with ancestry through geography?** Geography shapes both: populations that live close together tend to share a climate and also share ancestry. Cold populations sit mostly at high latitudes, where the samples come from Eurasia, so a population's climate partly tells you its continent. If continental regions occupy distinct zones of climate, an analysis cannot easily separate the effect of climate from the effect of shared ancestry. The statistical correction for relatedness then risks removing part of the real climate signal together with the ancestry signal.

2.  **Can temperature be separated from day length?** Day length follows latitude exactly, because the annual photoperiod range is set by geometry. Temperature follows latitude only loosely, because altitude, continentality (distance from the sea) and ocean currents also matter. The two can be told apart only where populations break the latitude–temperature pattern, so the question is how many populations do so, and which ones. The sample also limits where those populations can come from: every population at or above 40° absolute latitude is Eurasian, and 14 of the 15 are European or East Asian. Any day-length contrast the figures show will therefore be mostly a contrast between Europe and East Asia, and cannot be generalized to other regions. This ties the question to the first one: the populations that carry the day-length contrast are the Eurasian ones, so day length is also entangled with ancestry.

3.  **How much does coordinate imprecision move the climate values?** HGDP coordinates give an approximate location for each population, not an exact sampling site. `r n_whole` of the `r n_pops` coordinates are recorded only to the nearest whole degree, so the true location may be up to about 55 km away in latitude. The climate maps, in contrast, resolve about 1 km. The question is which climate values stay stable across that uncertainty, and which sit on gradients (such as mountains and coasts) so steep that the value at a single point depends on exactly where it falls.

# Approach

I will build a Shiny app that explores the three questions with interactive figures. The scripts in the repository download the data and have already built the tables that the app will use, so anyone can rerun them and get the same figures.

The final written-up, made in Quarto with the code visible, will answer each question with a static ggplot figure. The Shiny app is a companion that allows readers to switch climate variables, try other circle sizes and follow one population across the linked figures. The report will link to the app, but can be read without it.

## Decision criteria

I treat 1 $^\circ$C of annual mean temperature as a meaningful difference. It corresponds to about 150 m of elevation at the standard lapse rate of 6.5 $^\circ$C per km (U.S. Standard Atmosphere 1976). The initial criteria are:

**Question 1**: two populations share a climate if their annual mean temperatures differ by less than 1 $^\circ$C. Climate is separable from ancestry if at least half of the populations share a climate with a population from another continent (all three Eurasian regions count as one).

**Question 2**: temperature and day length can be separated if the correlation between annual mean temperature and annual photoperiod range is 0.7 or less in absolute value. Both would be predictors in the same genetic model, and above that level collinearity between predictors begins to distort model estimates (Dormann et al. 2013). Populations whose temperature lies more than 3 $^\circ$C above or below a linear trend line of temperature on latitude (with a LOESS curve as a check) are the ones that can separate the two. Their temperature differs from what their latitude predicts by three times the meaningful difference, which is more than coordinate or climate-surface error would usually explain.

**Question 3**: a population’s temperature is sensitive if its 50 km circle mean differs from the point value by 1 $^\circ$C or more, the meaningful difference defined above. A coordinate recorded without decimals (for example, 36$^\circ$N) could really lie anywhere between 35.5$^\circ$ and 36.5$^\circ$, up to about 55 km away, so the 50 km circle covers roughly where the population could be. Coordinates are precise enough if no more than 5 populations (about 10%) are sensitive; in that case I will use the circle mean for those populations. If more are sensitive, I will use circle means for all populations, since point values are not a reliable way to assign climate in this study.

These thresholds are set from general considerations, not from the results. I will check each one against the data before making the final figures. I will revise a criterion only if it cannot tell the possible answers apart, and never because of the answer it gives. Any change, and the reason for it, will be reported in the write-up.

## Planned figures 

Regions will keep the same color in all figures, using the Okabe–Ito palette, which is safe for color-blind readers and has exactly seven colors plus black. When space permits, regions and labeled populations will be named directly in the figure rather than only in a legend.

- **Figure for Question 1 (climate, ancestry and geography):** a dot plot with one row per continental region and one dot per population, placed by its annual mean temperature. Where dots of different regions fall at the same temperature, those populations share a climate but come from different regions, so climate can be compared without region (a rough proxy for ancestry) changing at the same time. Temperatures where only one region has dots cannot be separated from region. A dropdown will switch to other climate variables, and a small world map will show where the populations are.

- **Figure for Question 2 (temperature and day length):** a scatterplot of absolute latitude against annual mean temperature, with one dot per population, colored by region, and a linear trend line (with a LOESS curve as a check; see Decision criteria). A tight trend will mean temperature and day length cannot be separated. Populations far from the line are the ones that can separate them. These populations will be labeled. A second scatterplot will show annual photoperiod range against temperature seasonality in the same way.

- **Figure for Question 3 (coordinate imprecision):** a map of the selected population with a circle around it (a buffer: the area within a given distance of the point), whose radius is set with a slider (0, 10, 25, 50, 75 or 100 km). A line plot will show how its annual mean temperature changes as the circle grows, starting from the value at the point. A dumbbell plot of all populations (one row each, with a dot for the value at the point and a dot for the circle mean, joined by a line) will be sorted by the size of the difference, so the populations at the top of the plot will be the ones whose coordinates matter most. Together, these plots will show how much a population's climate changes if its coordinate is off by up to 100 km. 

**Audience**. To use this app, no background in genomics is needed. To help with interpretation, I will include a brief explanation indicating what each figure represents and which pattern would be problematic for the study design. Specific terms such as annual photoperiod range and buffer will be defined the first time they appear, and a short explanation of the POLYCLOCK question will also be added. 

## What is new to me

For this class I am teaching myself three new skills: working with maps, buffers and raster data in the `terra` package; building an interactive app with Shiny; and deploying the app so that others can access it. Before writing this proposal, I used `terra` (with the `geodata` package for the download) to extract the climate data and build the climate tables (`scripts/02_climate_data.R`). After the proposal is revised, Shiny and deployment will be the main focus.

In class we made maps with `sf`, which works with vector data such as points and polygons. My climate data are rasters: grids of about 1 km cells covering the whole world. `terra` is built for rasters, reads the large map files from disk without loading them into memory, and lets me take the mean of the cells inside a circle, weighting each cell by how much of it lies inside. That weighted mean is what makes the circle comparison for Question 3 possible, and `sf` alone cannot do it.

## Potential challenges

- **Learning Shiny in three weeks.** Shiny is new to me. First, I will make a static version of each figure so that the project has complete results even if some interactive features are removed. Linking the figures is planned only if time allows, so that would be the first feature I would remove.

- **Deploying the app** The application must run on a server with its data and packages. The climate maps (approximately 10 GB) are too large to upload, so the application will take its climate values from the small derived tables. The maps in the application will be simple background maps with the populations and the circle drawn on them, not temperature-colored maps. I have set aside time to test the application from another computer.

- **Imperfect data.** One coordinate (Adygei) is located at sea and has no climate value at that point, so I will use its 25 km circle mean instead. Some mountain populations have temperature values that vary by several degrees over tens of kilometers. These cases are part of what Question 3 shows, so I will keep them in the data and highlight them, rather than removing them.
